lead: This unit links transmission-line theory to the hardware that carries RF and microwaves: lines, printed boards, waveguides and resonators. After it you can compute Z0, reflection, VSWR and input impedance, match a load with a quarter-wave section or stub, read a Smith chart, and choose waveguide modes and resonator Q.
about: The unit starts with distributed line parameters and the telegrapher's equations in 1.1, then uses the reflected wave to define Γ, standing waves and VSWR in 1.2. Chapter 1.3 turns these waves into input impedance for open, short and loaded lines. Chapter 1.4 applies that impedance idea to quarter-wave and stub matching, while 1.5 gives the Smith chart as a graphical tool for the same calculations. Chapter 1.6 moves from cables to printed microstrip and stripline. Chapter 1.7 treats hollow rectangular and circular waveguides with TE and TM modes, and 1.8 closes with microwave resonators and Q.

chapters.idea: Distributed R, L, G and C per metre lead to the telegrapher's equations, whose solution gives Z0, propagation constant, wavelength and velocity.
chapters.depth: Primary constants R (Ω/m), L (H/m), G (S/m), C (F/m); telegrapher's equations; general solution V = V⁺e^(−γz) + V⁻e^(γz); secondary constants γ = α + jβ and Z0; lossless Z0 = √(L/C), β = ω√(LC), vp = 1/√(LC), λ = 2π/β; infinite line; waveform distortion and distortionless condition R/L = G/C; loading methods; line not terminated in Z0; current, voltage, power and transmission efficiency; some syllabi call R, L, G, C the primary line constants.

figure.aria: Primary line constants feed the telegrapher equations, whose solution gives Z0, γ, wavelength and velocity.

chapters.example: A lossless line has L = 0.25 μH/m and C = 100 pF/m. Find Z0, vp and λ at 100 MHz. Z0 = √(L/C) = 50 Ω; vp = 1/√(LC) = 2×10⁸ m/s; λ = vp/f = 2 m.
chapters.trap: Using free-space c for vp and forgetting that R and G make Z0 complex; also mixing per-metre values with total L or C.
chapters.prereq: Basic circuit theory, phasors and complex numbers.
chapters.leave: Reflection coefficient to 1.2; input impedance to 1.3; matching to 1.4; waveguide modes to 1.7.

chapters.idea: A load mismatch creates a reflected wave, and the sum of forward and reflected waves gives standing waves, reflection coefficient and VSWR.
chapters.depth: Γ at load ΓL = (ZL−Z0)/(ZL+Z0); at distance d, Γ(d) = ΓL e^(−j2βd) on a lossless line; voltage and current standing waves; VSWR = (1+|Γ|)/(1−|Γ|); return loss = −20 log10|Γ| dB; reflection factor and reflection loss; reflected power |Γ|² and transmitted power 1−|Γ|²; current, voltage, power delivered and efficiency for a mismatched line.

figure.title: Standing wave on a mismatched line
figure.aria: Voltage magnitude along a line with a real reflection coefficient of 0.5 rises to 1.5 and falls to 0.5 every quarter wavelength.

chapters.example: A 50 Ω line ends in ZL = 100 + j50 Ω. Find Γ, VSWR, return loss and reflected power fraction. Γ = (50 + j50)/(150 + j50) = 0.4 + j0.2; |Γ| = 0.447; VSWR = 1.447/0.553 = 2.62; return loss = 6.99 dB; reflected power fraction = 0.20.
chapters.trap: Forgetting that Γ is complex and changes phase along the line; calling return loss negative; using VSWR = (1−|Γ|)/(1+|Γ|).
chapters.leave: Input impedance and open/short lines to 1.3; stub positions to 1.4; Smith chart rotation to 1.5.

chapters.idea: The impedance seen at a line input depends on load and electrical length, so open and short lines become reactances and λ/4 or λ/2 sections transform a load.
chapters.depth: Lossless input impedance Zin = Z0(ZL + jZ0 tan βd)/(Z0 + jZL tan βd); electrical length βd = 2πd/λ; open and short line reactance; λ/4 inversion and λ/2 repeat; input and transfer impedance; low-loss factor e^(−2αd); power and efficiency.

figure.aria: A load and an electrical line length feed the Zin formula, which gives special open, short and matched cases.

chapters.example: A 50 Ω line has ZL = 100 + j50 Ω and length d = λ/8. Find Zin. βd = π/4 and tan βd = 1; Zin = 50(100 + j50 + j50)/(50 + j(100 + j50)) = 50 − j50 Ω.
chapters.trap: Using tan with degrees; forgetting that a λ/2 line repeats ZL and a λ/4 line inverts it; ignoring loss on a long line.
chapters.leave: Matching design to 1.4; graphical reading to 1.5; cavity resonance to 1.8.

chapters.idea: A quarter-wave section transforms a real load, and a stub cancels load reactance so the input looks like Z0.
chapters.depth: Quarter-wave transformer Z0' = √(Z0ZL) for real ZL; single-stub shunt and series matching; open and short stubs; location d and stub length l; bandwidth and tolerance; impedance matching methods and bandwidth optimization criteria; some syllabi call the λ/4 section a quarter-wave matching section.

figure.aria: A 50 Ω source feeds a quarter-wave section of 70.7 Ω, which matches a 100 Ω real load.

chapters.example: Match a 100 Ω resistive load to a 50 Ω line with a quarter-wave transformer at 2.4 GHz. Find Z0' and the physical length if vp = 2×10⁸ m/s. Z0' = √(50×100) = 70.7 Ω; λ = vp/f = 8.33 cm; λ/4 = 2.08 cm.
chapters.trap: Using a quarter-wave transformer on a complex load without cancelling reactance first; measuring stub length from the source; using c/f instead of vp/f.
chapters.leave: Smith chart construction to 1.5; microstrip realization to 1.6; filter design to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: The Smith chart maps normalized impedance to the reflection-coefficient plane, turning line rotation and matching into a graphical construction.
chapters.depth: Normalized impedance z = Z/Z0; Γ = (z−1)/(z+1); constant resistance and reactance circles; VSWR circles; admittance chart; rotation 2βd toward generator; reading Zin, Γ, VSWR, stub position and stub length.

figure.aria: The Smith chart procedure normalizes a load, plots its reflection point, draws a VSWR circle, rotates by line length and reads the match.

chapters.example: A 50 Ω line ends in ZL = 100 + j50 Ω. Use the Smith chart idea to find Γ, VSWR and normalized load. zL = 2 + j1; Γ = (zL−1)/(zL+1) = 0.4 + j0.2; |Γ| = 0.447; VSWR = 2.62.
chapters.trap: Plotting ZL without normalizing by Z0; rotating the wrong way; confusing impedance and admittance scales.
chapters.leave: Hardware matching to 1.4; resonator Q to 1.8; S-parameters to Unit 4.

chapters.idea: Microstrip, stripline and coplanar lines guide fields in printed metal and dielectric layers, with effective permittivity setting Z0 and wavelength.
chapters.depth: Microstrip, stripline and coplanar lines; effective permittivity εeff; approximate microstrip Z0 and εeff design formulas; field confinement; conductor, dielectric and radiation loss; dispersion; skin effect; use in MIC and MMIC; some syllabi call these printed transmission lines.

figure.aria: Microstrip cross-section: a strip conductor on a dielectric of thickness h above a ground plane.

chapters.example: A microstrip has εr = 4.4, h = 1.6 mm and W = 3 mm. Find W/h, εeff and Z0. W/h = 1.875; εeff = 3.32; Z0 ≈ 50.8 Ω.
chapters.trap: Using εr instead of εeff; treating microstrip as pure TEM; ignoring dispersion and loss at high frequency.
chapters.prereq: 1.1 for Z0 and 1.3 for line impedance.
chapters.leave: Patch antenna design to Unit 3; S-parameters and MMIC to Unit 4; high-frequency device models to Unit 5.

chapters.idea: Hollow metal waveguides support TE and TM modes only above cutoff, and dimensions plus mode indices set cutoff, guide wavelength and velocity.
chapters.depth: Rectangular waveguide cutoff fc = (c/(2√εr))√((m/a)²+(n/b)²); TE and TM modes; TE10 dominant mode; λc = 2/√((m/a)²+(n/b)²); λg = λ/√(1−(fc/f)²); phase and group velocity; wave impedance; circular waveguide TE11 dominant mode and Bessel-root cutoff; field patterns.

figure.title: TE10 guide wavelength
figure.aria: TE10 guide wavelength falls toward the free-space wavelength as frequency rises above cutoff.

chapters.example: An air-filled rectangular waveguide has a = 2.286 cm and b = 1.016 cm. Find fc of TE10, TE20 and TE01, and λg at 10 GHz for TE10. fc10 = c/(2a) = 6.56 GHz; fc20 = 13.12 GHz; fc01 = c/(2b) = 14.76 GHz; λg = 3/√(1−(6.56/10)²) cm = 3.97 cm.
chapters.trap: Using λ0 in place of λg; thinking a mode propagates below cutoff; forgetting that TM modes need both indices nonzero.
chapters.leave: Waveguide tees, couplers and S-parameters to Unit 4; horn and aperture antennas to Unit 3; cavity Q to 1.8.

chapters.idea: Microwave resonators store energy at a resonant frequency, and Q compares stored energy with loss to set bandwidth.
chapters.depth: Series and parallel RLC resonance; f0 = 1/(2π√LC); Q = ω0 × stored energy / power loss; unloaded, loaded and external Q; 1/QL = 1/Q0 + 1/Qe; QL = f0/BW for a bandpass resonator; rectangular cavity modes; λ/2 and λ/4 line resonators; dielectric and microstrip resonators; loss and temperature drift.

figure.title: Loaded resonator response
figure.aria: A resonator response peaks at f0 and falls to 0.707 at f0 plus or minus 1 percent for QL equal to 100.

chapters.example: A resonator has f0 = 2 GHz and bandwidth 20 MHz. Find QL. If unloaded Q0 = 500, find external Qe. QL = f0/BW = 100; 1/100 = 1/500 + 1/Qe; Qe = 125.
chapters.trap: Using unloaded Q for bandwidth when the resonator is connected to a load; writing Q = BW/f0; forgetting that a shorted λ/4 line resonates as a parallel circuit.
chapters.leave: Filter synthesis to Unit 4; oscillator phase noise to Unit 5; antenna bandwidth to Unit 2.
